analysis.one_liner: Retrofit public schools to zero carbon, fund school staff and disability education with roughly $1.5 trillion over ten years.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2026 with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to two House committees and has seen no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create several grant programs to make public schools zero-carbon and healthy, with full federal funding for retrofits at the most vulnerable third of schools and Bureau of Indian Education schools. It would also send $250 billion over ten years to hire counselors, nurses, social workers, paraprofessionals, and teachers in understaffed schools, make disability education funding mandatory and rising, and add $74 billion a year for Title I aid to low-income schools. Construction work would be covered by prevailing-wage rules, local hiring targets, and domestic-content requirements.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and staff in under-resourced and climate-vulnerable schools get modernized buildings with clean air, safe water, and heat, plus far more counselors, nurses, psychologists, and teachers. School districts with high poverty get the full cost of retrofits covered. Construction and clean-energy workers get a decade of federally funded work at prevailing wages with apprenticeship and local-hiring preferences, and communities with poor air quality and high pollution get at least half of the $4 billion-a-year resiliency grants.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and staff at under-resourced schools

how_it_helps.text: Provides $446 billion in grants, plus up to $446 billion in zero- or low-interest loans, to retrofit or build zero-carbon schools, covering 100 percent of the cost for schools ranked in the most vulnerable third and for Bureau of Indian Education schools.

Provides $250 billion over ten years to hire and pay educators and support staff, including paraprofessionals, mental health professionals, counselors, nurses, librarians, and teachers, with goals of one counselor and one social worker per 250 students and one psychologist per 500 students.

Makes Individuals with Disabilities Education Act funding mandatory, ramping from about $6.4 billion in fiscal 2027 to $69.6 billion, or 40 percent of the national average per-pupil cost, each year thereafter.
Appropriates $74 billion a year for ten years for Title I aid to low-income schools, in addition to existing appropriations.

Provides $4 billion a year in climate resiliency grants, with at least half required to go to environmental justice communities, for projects like electric school buses, backup power, flood protection, and universal school internet.

Requires prevailing wages under the Davis-Bacon Act, project labor agreements on projects of $25 million or more, at least 20 percent registered apprentices, Buy American materials, and a plan to hire at least 30 percent of grant-funded jobs from the local community.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the full cost, roughly $1.4 to $1.5 trillion over ten years, because the money is appropriated directly out of the Treasury rather than through the normal annual budget process, adding to federal deficits unless offset elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes most of its roughly $1.5 trillion in spending mandatory appropriations for a decade, bypassing the annual review where Congress normally weighs school funding against other priorities and could adjust it.
Districts must promise to keep the federally funded staff positions on their own budgets after the ten-year grant period ends, a commitment many high-poverty districts may struggle to keep.

Grantees face extensive planning, reporting, and labor-standard requirements, including community-engaged plans and public data dashboards, which could delay aid to smaller districts with little administrative capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets money carefully at the schools and students with the greatest need and pairs it with job standards that steer the work to local and unionized labor, which is an unusually detailed design. The honest objection is the price and process: more than $1.4 trillion in mandatory spending over a decade, locked in without annual review, at a moment when neither chamber has shown interest in it. The benefits to students and workers would be large if it passed; the fiscal cost is also real.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced; neither has scheduled a hearing or vote, and it sits there while the 119th Congress continues through January 2027.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill on July 27, 2026, with 14 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
A total of 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, signed on; no Republican cosponsors appear.
The bill was referred that day to the Education and Workforce Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, splitting jurisdiction between them.
Since referral, the action history shows no hearings, markups, amendments, or votes of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost; the bill has not advanced. If it dies without a vote at the end of the 119th Congress, opponents of large mandatory federal school spending will have prevailed by default, and current school funding and school energy arrangements will continue unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill has only been referred

sides.party_line_note: All 18 supporters of the bill are Democrats and no Republican cosponsors signed on; the Republican-led committees to which it was referred have not moved it.

industries.note: A decade of $446 billion in grants plus loans for school retrofits and new construction would be a huge source of work. The jobs carry strings that mostly favor workers: prevailing wages, project labor agreements on large jobs, apprenticeship quotas, and local hiring targets.

industries.industry: Clean energy and building electrification manufacturers and installers
industries.note: Zero-carbon schools must be all-electric with onsite solar and storage, electric school buses, and heat-pump-era kitchens, creating a decade of demand. Buy American and domestic-content rules require the equipment to be made in the United States, steering that demand to domestic plants.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and school-energy suppliers
industries.note: The bill converts school heating, cooking, and buses to electricity and bars newly built schools from sitting within 2,500 feet of oil or gas wells, cutting schools out of the market for fossil fuel energy. The loss to the industry comes directly from the cleaner-air benefit to students.

industries.industry: Building trades unions and registered apprenticeship programs
industries.note: The bill requires prevailing wages and union-negotiated project labor agreements on projects of $25 million or more and requires contractors to show they can staff projects with at least 20 percent registered apprentices, channeling the construction work through union training pipelines.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a House Republican majority, and no committee action in the months since referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing, markup, or floor vote and will most likely sit in committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
